clue.text: se a blindfold to lead solvers up the garden path?

definitions.text: se a blindfold to lead solvers up the garden path?

parts.note: surface reading: literally covering someone's sight with a strip of cloth

parts.words: to lead solvers up the garden path?
parts.note: setter's reading: the idiom for deceiving someone, pictured as covering their vision with fleece

annotation.spelling: PULL THE WOOL OVER ONE'S EYES

explanation.surface: A setter confesses to hoodwinking the people doing the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as received has lost its first letter; it should read 'Use a blindfold'. The phrase is pictured literally, a woollen cover over the face.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to deceive or hoodwink somebody, just as leading them up the garden path means misleading them.

clue.text: Strange one!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: odd, remarkable, out of the ordinary
second meaning: the grammatical number for a single item, as opposed to plural

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation makes it read as a remark about some odd person; 'one' is really the grammar term for a single thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Singular can describe something peculiar or unusual, and in grammar it is the form denoting exactly a single item.

clue.text: One with inside knowledge set up the fiesta

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, so the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: one is the indefinite article a
a lag is a convict, someone who knows life 'inside' prison

explanation.surface: An insider has organised the festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' is British slang for in prison, and an old lag is a habitual convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive public celebration, which is what a Spanish fiesta is.

clue.text: See 10
Map makers lean to port

parts.note: the Ordnance Survey, Britain's official mapping agency
to tend to something is to be inclined or lean towards it

explanation.surface: Cartographers seem to tilt their charts towards a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean to' looks like a shed; it is the verb phrase for being inclined. Ostend is a Belgian ferry port.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a seaport on the Belgian coast, long linked by ferry to England.

clue.text: One takes pains to avoid amphetamine pills and Swiss pot

parts.note: E is ecstasy, an amphetamine-type drug, and the pills are several of them
CH is the international code for Switzerland
a ewer is a large jug or pitcher

explanation.surface: Someone careful to keep away from drugs: speed, pills and Swiss cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' tempts as cannabis alongside the pills; it is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew is to shun deliberately, so an eschewer is a person who makes a point of keeping clear of something.

clue.text: Friends, perhaps, arrive shortly after rest

indicators.note: done shortly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter
after places the second piece behind the first in reading order

parts.note: to sit is to rest
to come is to arrive

explanation.surface: Some pals turn up soon after a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Friends, with a capital F hidden at the start of the clue, is the American TV comedy series.
explanation.definitionFit: Friends is a famous example of a situation comedy, hence the 'perhaps' marking it as an instance.

clue.text: Have known better days to chance upon Dickens' work

parts.note: to fall on something is to come across it by chance
Hard Times is a novel by Charles Dickens

explanation.surface: Someone down on their luck happens upon a Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall on hard times is to become poor after prosperity, i.e. to be past one's better days.

clue.text: Just a single parent

parts.note: surface reading: a lone mother or father bringing up children
setter's reading: a parent that produces only one offspring at each birth

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests a one-parent family; the answer is the biological term for bearing one young at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes animals that bring forth only one offspring per birth, so such a mother is a parent of just one.

clue.text: Tell a tall tale and get the thread of it?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to tell an entertaining, embroidered story
second meaning, taken literally: to make fine thread by spinning fibre

explanation.surface: A storyteller embroiders a tale and asks whether listeners follow the plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the thread' sounds like following a story; read literally it is producing yarn on a spinning wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means narrating an engaging story, while literally twisting fibre produces yarn, which is thread.

clue.text: Rider, first away, wins 1 pound following the others …

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the adjective, lagging behind

indicators.note: first away tells us the opening letter is removed from the name
to win something is to gain it, so the name acquires an extra piece in front

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for one pound
H. Rider Haggard wrote King Solomon's Mines

explanation.surface: A jockey, slow away from the start, still collects a pound while trailing the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rider' looks like a jockey, which suits 'following the others'; it is the author's middle name.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard straggler is slow and falls behind, so it describes something coming along after everyone else.

clue.text: … and the others must inspire Gothic endings

definitions.note: a modal verb standing for the adjective: what one is morally bound to do

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: et al. is the Latin abbreviation for 'and others'

indicators.note: endings points to the closing letters of the word, keeping its tail

parts.note: the final three letters of the word

explanation.surface: Continuing from the clue before, the rest of the field must draw inspiration from Gothic conclusions.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 11; 'must' is the loose definition, what conscience obliges.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical concerns moral duty, the sense of what a person ought or is obliged to do.

clue.text: Ready to drop ad?

definitions.note: a reverse clue: these two letters are one half of a four-letter word for lifeless
definitions.meaning: second meaning: these letters are the latter ... of a word meaning lifeless

explanation.surface: Someone exhausted wonders whether to pull an advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ad' looks like an advertisement being dropped; it is literally half of DEAD, its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being half dead means being so tired one is fit to collapse, as is someone ready to drop.

clue.text: Jill of all trades — and how many, roughly

indicators.note: roughly means approximately or crudely made, so the letters come out in a rough new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking how many versatile women there are, at a rough count.
explanation.walkthrough: Jill of all trades is the feminine twist on 'Jack of all trades'.
explanation.definitionFit: A handywoman does all sorts of small repairs and jobs, a female counterpart of the versatile Jack of all trades.

clue.text: Labourer came first to invest the fluctuating mark

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to come first in a contest is to win it

indicators.note: fluctuating means shifting about, so these letters change position

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A worker won the race and put his money into the unstable Deutschmark.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about currency speculation: the mark was the German currency.
explanation.definitionFit: A workman is a man employed in manual labour, a direct synonym for a labourer.

clue.text: Mind clumsy sommelier dropping second claret?

indicators.note: clumsy means awkwardly handled, so the letters are jumbled
dropping means letting fall, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: second picks out the letter in position two of the following word

parts.note: its second letter

explanation.surface: Watch out: the awkward wine waiter is about to spill the claret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind' reads as a warning; here it is the verb meaning to keep in memory.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind can mean to remember or keep in one's head, which is what committing something to memory does.

clue.text: Narco ends off being overwhelmed by Brave New World drug growth

indicators.note: something overwhelmed is engulfed, so it sits inside the other piece
with both ends off, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: soma is the happiness drug in Aldous Huxley's novel
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drug baron is swamped by the rise of a fictional narcotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth' seems to belong with the drug trade; it is the definition, a tumour.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarcoma is a malignant tumour of connective tissue, and a tumour is a growth.

clue.text: Superlatively unctuous list re-drawn to accommodate van der Rohe

indicators.note: to accommodate is to house or take in, so the other piece goes inside
a list drawn up again comes out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
the architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe

explanation.surface: The most oily list of architects is revised to fit in a famous modernist.
explanation.definitionFit: Slimy can mean obsequious or oily in manner, and the -est form makes it the most unctuous.

clue.text: See 1
Confident? Some nerve! I'm first to be taken in

indicators.note: taken in means admitted inside, so these pieces go within the other

parts.note: the optic nerve is one particular nerve
taken as written
1st written with I for the figure one

explanation.surface: Someone cocky boasts of having the nerve to go in first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some nerve!' reads as an exclamation at cheek; it means one nerve of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: An optimistic person is hopeful and sure things will turn out well, i.e. confident.

clue.text: Stomach having to accept journalist (not Hill) displaying monotony

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece receives the other

parts.note: tum is an informal word for the stomach

indicators.note: not means without, so the word for a hill is taken away

parts.note: an editor is a senior journalist

explanation.surface: Someone who can stomach a reporter, so long as it isn't one named Hill, is bored.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hill, so EDITOR without TOR leaves EDI.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedium is wearisome sameness, which is exactly what monotony is.

clue.text: Probe away to capture revolting peasant? Not right!

indicators.note: to capture is to hold prisoner, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: read as 'a way': St, short for street, is a way

indicators.note: not right means without R, the abbreviation for right, so that letter goes

parts.note: Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381

explanation.surface: A search party sets out to seize a rebel peasant, but it is told it has got the wrong one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away' must be split into 'a way', giving ST for street. Wat Tyler was the leader of England's Peasants' Revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylet is a slender surgical instrument used for probing, so it is itself a probe.

clue.text: See 13
Bristol fashion porter

definitions.meaning: first meaning: neat and tidy, from the nautical 'shipshape and Bristol fashion'
second meaning: a hospital attendant who moves patients and equipment

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a style of beer from Bristol; 'shipshape and Bristol fashion' is a British phrase for neatly ordered.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly as an adjective means tidy and well arranged; as a noun it names a hospital attendant like a porter.

clue.text: Sharon is raising kings in 11

indicators.note: raising means lifting up, which in a clue read across turns the word back to front
in places the preceding piece inside the following one

parts.note: the figures one and one written as two I's
Lear is a king of Shakespeare's, and kings are several of him

explanation.surface: Sharon is lifting the kings at position eleven, like a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like a cross-reference to 11 across, but it is two ones, written II. Ariel Sharon was an Israeli general and prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariel Sharon was a citizen and leader of Israel, so he is an example of the nationality.

clue.text: Barney's rackets

definitions.note: read as the plural barneys, quarrels
definitions.meaning: first meaning: noisy quarrels; a barney is British slang for a squabble

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as rackets belonging to someone called Barney, as for tennis; a barney is British slang for a noisy argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Rows are heated quarrels, the same as barneys, and a row is also a loud noise, as is a racket.

clue.text: Take note of queues forming for Shaffer's play

indicators.note: forming means taking shape, so the remaining letters are arranged into something new
take something of a word means remove it, so that letter comes out

parts.note: E is a musical note
taken as written

explanation.surface: Be aware of the lines forming outside the theatre for a Peter Shaffer play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take note of' reads as 'notice'; here it means remove a note, E, from the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Equus is the 1973 stage drama by Peter Shaffer about a boy who blinds horses.

clue.text: Freewheels before getting to another place

indicators.note: free means loose and unrestrained, so the letters are let go to rearrange

parts.note: the word splits in two; after the signal word come these six letters
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A cyclist coasts downhill on the way to somewhere new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freewheels' looks like one word; it splits into the indicator and the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsewhere means in or to a different location, i.e. some other place.
